---
description: "Performance guidance for NCodeGroup code: keep request paths bounded and free of avoidable I/O and allocations, cache and fetch shared data safely, require benchmarks for hot-primitive optimizations, and skip performance findings that have no measured cost."
applyTo: "**/*.cs, **/*.csproj, **/Directory.Build.props, **/*.ts, **/*.tsx, **/*.ps1, **/*.psm1, **/.github/workflows/**"
---

# Performance

<!-- Generated by `npm run train` from the sources each rule cites. To change a rule for good, change its source or say so in training/feedback.md; the next training run regenerates this file. -->

- **Build in-memory cache keys from registration or configuration values. When a cache's keys come from request input or from values a tenant or caller controls, bound the cache, for example with a size limit or with idle expiry that disposes entries.** If callers control the keys, they can grow memory, connection pools and background refreshes without limit for the life of the process. *Check:* Look for caches or long-lived dictionaries keyed by query strings, headers, route values, body fields or tenant identities that have no size limit or expiry and are cleared only on Dispose. <sub>Identity ADR-1381; Identity outcomes of #584</sub>
- **In production code, never run work that grows with the data or the deployment (a pass over every record, tenant, client or team) inside a request or on a bounded in-process job dispatcher. Run it as a paged background pass on one replica that reads lightweight projections and never loads a whole hierarchy into memory.** Such work makes request latency grow without limit and ties up the dispatcher's bounded workers. *Check:* Look for full-table scans, loops over all tenants or entities in request handlers, unpaged reads of whole sets, or such passes queued on an in-process job dispatcher. *Applies to:* `**/*.cs` <sub>Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Don't fetch entities with one store call per id or per item in a loop. Gather the keys, for example over one page of items, and read them in a single batched get-many query.** Per-item calls cost one database round trip per entity, so the number of round trips grows with the input. *Check:* Look for `await store.GetOrDefaultAsync(id)` or a similar awaited store call inside a `foreach` over ids or page items whose keys could be read in one call. <sub>Identity outcomes of #585; Identity outcomes of #599</sub>
- **Reuse data the current operation already holds. Use a lineage or parent entity the method has already read, check entities the DbContext already tracks (`DbSet.Local`) before querying in a load-then-update flow, and memoize an answer that several places in one request ask for, including a negative answer, in `HttpContext.Items`.** Resolving data again turns one read into many queries, and one memoized answer keeps later callers consistent, such as an audit step that runs after commit when the row may be gone. *Check:* Look for loops that call a store-backed resolve or count method for each element the method just read, store methods that re-query entities the unit of work already loaded, and per-request resolvers that read the store again for a caller they already answered or cache only positive answers. <sub>Identity outcomes of #599; Identity ADR-1012; Identity ADR-1466</sub>
- **In a request handler, run a lookup whose result only feeds a later step, such as an audit record, after input validation has passed.** Running it first adds a query to every request, including requests that then fail validation. *Check:* Look for a store or database query placed before a validate call when its result is used only after validation succeeds. <sub>Identity outcomes of #839</sub>
- **Start independent async reads together and await them with `Task.WhenAll`, not one after another in a loop.** Awaiting each read in turn against a networked provider adds one round trip per read to every request. *Check:* Look for a loop that awaits one read per iteration where no iteration depends on an earlier result. <sub>coordination outcomes of #22</sub>
- **Don't hold a per-key lock or `SemaphoreSlim` on the request path while making a series of remote round trips, such as one KMS unwrap per row. Limit the work to what the request needs, or move it outside the lock or into a background service.** The first request waits for N round trips, and every concurrent request for the same key queues behind it. *Check:* Look for loops of awaited remote calls inside a held lock or semaphore on a request path. <sub>Identity outcomes of #572</sub>
- **Fetch a shared remote resource (metadata document, key set, revocation list, caller-supplied URL) through one in-flight fetch per key, for example a self-removing `ConcurrentDictionary<TKey, Lazy<Task<T>>>` entry. Bound that fetch with its own timeout, not a caller's token. Callers wait with `WaitAsync`.** Concurrent misses otherwise send one fetch per caller, and one caller cancelling must not cancel the fetch that everyone else is waiting on. *Check:* Look for shared fetches that start once per concurrent caller or per request, or that pass a caller's CancellationToken into the shared fetch itself. <sub>Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity ADR-1285</sub>
- **Cache a failed shared or outbound retrieval (unreachable, timed out, non-2xx, oversized, malformed, refused, or empty) for a configured, positive failure duration. Don't start a new fetch while the failure is cached, and log each skipped fetch at debug level.** Without this, an unreachable endpoint costs a full timeout on every request, and a client that sends many requests makes the server send as many outbound fetches. The cached failure acts as the back-off. *Check:* Look for outbound fetches whose failures are not cached, whose failure duration is hard-coded instead of an option, whose cached failure still lets a new fetch start, or whose skipped fetches are not logged. <sub>Identity ADR-1106; Identity ADR-1259; Identity ADR-1400; Identity csharp.instructions.md</sub>
- **When a refresh of cached remote metadata or keys fails, serve the last good value only within a bounded stale lifetime and back off for a minimum interval. Rate-limit forced refreshes, such as one triggered by an unknown `kid`, by the same interval, and never relax validation to serve a stale value.** This bounds the load on the provider and the exposure to stale data, and a stale value can never bypass validation. *Check:* Look for stale values served with no age limit, forced refreshes with no rate limit, or a stale path that skips validation. <sub>Identity ADR-1285</sub>
- **Keep caches of large, rebuildable data fetched over the network, and the cached failures of those fetches, in a process-local `IMemoryCache`, not in a distributed or shared-state cache.** The data is large and can be rebuilt, and a network failure on one replica must not stop the other replicas. *Check:* Look for downloaded revocation lists, key sets or similar fetched data, or their cached failures, written to a distributed cache. <sub>Identity ADR-1400</sub>
- **Give each per-instance cache entry an absolute lifetime. Register eviction cleanup only for entries that own disposable native resources. Announce changes after commit as a best-effort, id-only hint whose failure is logged without failing the write, and drop entries that may be invalid after a reconnect.** An absolute lifetime bounds staleness without tying writes to messaging. Plain data, such as public keys, needs no disposal callback. *Check:* Look for cache entries with only sliding expiry, entries that hold native handles but have no eviction disposal, eviction callbacks on plain data, invalidation messages that carry data, and writes that fail when the announcement fails. <sub>Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity ADR-1106</sub>
- **When a broadcast subscription reports possibly missed messages, revalidate the cache instead of clearing it: compare each cached entry's row concurrency token with the store's current token, and evict only entries whose token differs or whose row no longer exists.** Clearing everything rebuilds every cached entry and repeats its store reads, mostly for changes that never happened. An equal token proves the cached copy is unchanged. *Check:* Look for missed-message handlers that clear every cache without comparing revisions, or that compare something other than the row's concurrency token. <sub>Identity ADR-1416</sub>
- **Page listings and reports over collections that can grow without limit. Return a normalized limit with a default and a maximum, plus a continuation token, and treat an empty page with a token still set as not the end. Serve each page by seeking an ordered index or reading only the requested prefix or partition, reading at most limit + 1 entries and sorting only the matches.** The work of one request must not grow with the size of the collection. Copying and sorting the whole store on every page makes paging quadratic and holds the store's lock while it runs. *Check:* Look for report or list endpoints that compute over every item in one request, page methods that snapshot, filter and sort the full set and then skip to the token, and callers that stop at an empty page while a token is still set. <sub>Identity ADR-1245; coordination outcomes of #19; coordination outcomes of #20</sub>
- **Walk a hierarchy with unbounded fan-out depth first, reading one bounded page of children per level. Don't read every descendant of a node as one list, and don't hold a whole level in a breadth-first walk.** A node can have any number of children, so a whole subtree or level can be arbitrarily large. A depth-first walk bounds memory by depth times page size. *Check:* Look for queries that return all descendants of a node at once, or breadth-first walks that hold a whole level in memory. <sub>Identity ADR-1426</sub>
- **Make a reconciliation pass that follows a change read only the items the change can affect, by comparing the previous and current settings. Fall back to reconciling every item only when the previous state is absent or unreadable.** A small change must not read the whole deployment. *Check:* Look for reconciliation handlers that enumerate all tenants or items without filtering by what changed. <sub>Identity ADR-1412</sub>
- **Don't remove elements one at a time with `RemoveAt` in a loop over a list or `JsonArray` whose size comes from input. Build the result in one pass into a pre-sized list.** Each `RemoveAt` shifts every later element, so a large input costs quadratic time. *Check:* Look for `RemoveAt(index)` inside a loop over a collection whose size comes from input. <sub>Identity outcomes of #552</sub>
- **Don't write audit or event records to the database inside the operation that raised them, and don't write per-request usage or accounting on the request path. Add the record to a bounded in-memory queue, or increment an in-memory counter under a lock, and have a hosted service flush to storage periodically in batches with a fixed maximum size.** An inline write adds a database round trip to every operation, and its failure fails the operation. Batching turns per-request write load into one small unit of work per replica per interval. *Check:* Look for event, audit or usage handlers that call a store, DbContext or SaveChanges, or await I/O, on the request path, and for flush batches with no fixed maximum size. <sub>Identity ADR-1303; Identity ADR-1199</sub>
- **When several rate limits apply to one request, check them in one batched, atomic call to the counter store that stops at the first limit exceeded. Check a quota and its overage allowance with one counter whose limit is the quota plus the allowance.** Sequential calls cost a round trip per limit. A pipeline can't stop at the first refusal, so a refused request still uses up later allowances. Compensating decrements leave an over-count that refuses other callers. A second overage counter adds state and a round trip. *Check:* Look for loops that await one store increment per limit, pipelined increments with no early stop, decrement-after-refusal logic, or a separate overage counter. <sub>Identity ADR-1246; Identity ADR-1198</sub>
- **In production code, exclude public metadata endpoints that anonymous callers or caches fetch (discovery, JWKS) from tenant quotas and billable usage. Record usage through the same mechanism that checks the rate limit, never through a separate usage-recording call next to the limit.** Anonymous fetches shouldn't use up a tenant's quota, and recording usage separately double-counts requests or counts refused ones. *Check:* Look for metered metadata endpoints, or direct usage-record calls in endpoints next to a limit check. *Applies to:* `**/*.cs` <sub>Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Serve JWKS and other public-key sets from cached public keys, not from a remote key management service or vault call on each request.** Each remote call adds a network round trip and costs money, and public keys can safely be cached. *Check:* Look for JWKS or public-key endpoints that call the KMS or vault client on every request with no cache. <sub>Identity docs/hosting-analysis.md</sub>
- **In production code, don't repeat certificate verification work on every request. Cache the verdict per certificate (for example by thumbprint plus trust-anchor generation, with an expiry no later than the certificate's validity and a size limit), parse configured values once, and check backing files for changes at most once per interval, outside any global lock.** Rebuilding an `X509Chain`, re-parsing options and checking a file's timestamp under a lock on every request adds syscalls, allocations and contention, even though a keep-alive connection presents the same certificate on every request. *Check:* Look for per-request verifiers that create an `X509Chain`, re-parse options, or call `File.GetLastWriteTimeUtc` inside a lock, and for verdict caches with no size or expiry limit. <sub>Identity outcomes of #794</sub>
- **When a token header's `kid` matches eligible decryption keys, try only those keys, not every candidate key.** A token that names its key then costs at most one service call per key. *Check:* Look for decryption key-selection loops that fall back to all keys even when a `kid` matches. <sub>Identity ADR-1472</sub>
- **When checking a supplied secret against several stored verifiers, try the verifiers with no work factor before any work-factor (KDF) verifier.** Checking them in storage order makes a wrong secret cost one full key derivation per stored verifier, which uses up hashing capacity and slows legitimate requests. *Check:* Look for verifier loops that run KDF-based verifiers before fast-hash ones, or that await every verifier in storage order. <sub>Identity ADR-1391; Identity outcomes of #531</sub>
- **Key a DPoP nonce cache by the request's origin (scheme, host and port), give it a fixed size limit, and clear it when it is full.** A server issues nonces per origin (RFC 9449 §8), the cache is in-process, and a stale or evicted nonce costs only one retry. *Check:* Look for nonce caches keyed by the full URI, or with no size limit. <sub>Identity ADR-1286</sub>
- **Extend a session's idle expiry only on real user activity, never on polling endpoints such as user-info, and only after a set fraction of the idle timeout has passed since the last write.** Polling then can't keep a session alive forever, and a busy session doesn't write to the store on every call. *Check:* Look for idle-expiry updates on every request or on polling and status endpoints. <sub>Identity ADR-1290</sub>
- **Make an existence check that runs on every configuration change answer without loading the resource, for example without reading key files or decoding keys.** Loading the resource reads every file on every change, and a load failure would reject the configuration for a reason the check's name doesn't show. *Check:* Look for configuration-change validators that load keys or read files only to find out whether a name exists. <sub>Identity ADR-1439</sub>
- **Serve content-hashed static assets from a file provider rooted at the assets folder, with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable` plus `ETag`, `Last-Modified` and range support, and send no cache lifetime on a `404`. In a multi-tenant host, serve public assets that are the same for every tenant from a route group that doesn't resolve the tenant.** A hashed file never changes under its name, but validators alone make the browser revalidate on every use. Rooting the provider keeps files outside the folder, `index.html` included, from being served. Resolving the tenant adds work and makes an unknown tenant's assets return `404`. *Check:* Look for hashed-asset handlers without the immutable one-year header or the validators, cache lifetimes on not-found responses, providers rooted above the assets folder, and asset routes that attach tenant resolution or tenant filters. <sub>Identity ADR-1193; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Cache a parsed build artifact, such as a bundle's index file, by its file version (last-write time and length), and check that metadata again on each request. Don't parse the file on every request, and don't use a file watcher to invalidate the cache.** The file changes once per build. A watcher holds an OS handle for the life of the host and behaves differently across container file systems. *Check:* Look for per-request reads or parses of a static index file, or a `FileSystemWatcher` or `IFileProvider.Watch` used to invalidate the cache. <sub>Identity ADR-1193</sub>
- **Return a materialized collection by default. Stream a large, unbounded, I/O-backed listing, such as paged remote or database results, as `IAsyncEnumerable<T>`, and return a lazy sequence only when it is large, unbounded, I/O-backed or usually cut short. Never return a lazy sequence that captures request state, or one the caller enumerates twice or counts.** Large remote listings shouldn't be held in memory all at once, while other lazy sequences repeat work and can outlive the state they capture. *Check:* Look for new methods that return `Task<List<T>>` or arrays for unbounded remote or database listings, and for `yield return` or deferred LINQ returned from methods that capture request state or whose results are enumerated more than once. <sub>Identity ADR-1478; Identity csharp.instructions.md</sub>
- **In production code on per-request paths, use `foreach` loops instead of LINQ (`Any`, `Where`, `Select`, `ToList`, `ToDictionary`, `Distinct`, `Order`) or collection-expression spreads. Fill collections held in named locals. Normalize a small set by copying it into one array, sorting in place with `Array.Sort` and an ordinal comparer, and compacting adjacent duplicates. Parse header and query values by splitting spans with `MemoryExtensions.Split` into a `Range` buffer, not with `string.Split`.** LINQ and `string.Split` allocate delegates, enumerators, sort buffers and substring arrays on every request. *Check:* Look for LINQ calls, `[.. x.Select(...)]` passed inline as arguments, and `string.Split` in middleware, handlers and other code that runs on each request or page render. *Note:* This covers per-call paths only. Code that runs once, such as startup parsing, is exempt (see the rule about not reporting allocations in run-once code). <sub>Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity outcomes of #547; Identity outcomes of #548; Identity outcomes of #839</sub>
- **Create a `List<T>`, `Dictionary<TKey,TValue>` or `HashSet<T>` with an initial capacity when its final or maximum count is already known, such as the source's `Count` or `Length`. Return a shared empty instance, such as `FrozenDictionary<TKey,TValue>.Empty`, instead of allocating a new empty collection.** A collection created without its known capacity resizes as it fills, and a new empty collection allocates on every read. *Check:* Look for `new List<T>()`, `new Dictionary<,>()` or `new HashSet<T>()` filled from a source whose count is available, and for a new empty collection returned for empty input. <sub>Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; Identity outcomes of #554; Identity outcomes of #577; Randomness outcomes of #12; coordination outcomes of #17</sub>
- **In production code on hot paths, check `Count == 0` before a `foreach` over an interface-typed collection, transform identifiers into rented `char` spans (for example with `MemoryExtensions.ToLowerInvariant(source, destination)`) instead of allocating new strings, and build per-element strings such as JSON Pointer paths only for the elements or error paths that use them.** Each of these avoids an allocation on every call: a boxed enumerator, a new string, or one path string per member that grows with depth. *Check:* Look for `foreach` over `IReadOnlyList`/`ICollection` with no empty check, `string.ToLowerInvariant()`/`ToUpperInvariant()` on per-request paths, and path or label strings built for every member of a walk. <sub>Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; Identity outcomes of #552</sub>
- **When the same hash function is applied to several values with the same output size in a row, allocate the output buffer once in the caller and pass it to each call. If that needs a `Span<byte>` inside an async method, move the work into a synchronous helper.** Reusing one buffer avoids repeated allocations, and dropping this reuse once caused a performance regression. *Check:* Look for consecutive hash computations (such as `at_hash`, `c_hash`, `s_hash`) where each call allocates or stackallocs its own buffer of the same size. <sub>Identity review of #341</sub>
- **Don't change one member of a JSON document by round-tripping it through text and several representations (string to `JsonNode` to string to `JsonElement`). Build the modified copy in one pass with a dedicated helper, for example one that uses `Utf8JsonWriter`, and remove error branches that can no longer run.** Round trips cost extra allocations and create a second construction path that has to be kept in step with the first. A `JsonObject` built from untrusted JSON can also throw on duplicate members. *Check:* Look for chains of `ToJsonString`/`JsonNode.Parse`/`JsonElement.Parse` used to add or replace one property, and for error branches that run after the input was already validated. <sub>Identity outcomes of #757</sub>
- **In the inner loops of cryptographic or numeric primitives that are aggressively optimized (`AggressiveInlining`/`AggressiveOptimization`, manual unrolling, `stackalloc`, `MemoryMarshal`/`Unsafe` reinterpretation, direct field access instead of span views over tiny fixed-limb structs), don't report readability problems. Do report any optimization that adds a branch or memory access that depends on secret data to constant-time code, or that lacks passing test vectors.** In these primitives speed comes before readability, but constant-time behaviour and correctness pinned by test vectors are never traded away. Direct field access is faster than a span view over a small struct. *Check:* In math or crypto primitive changes, look for branches or indexing that depend on secret data, missing test vectors, and span views created over small fixed-limb structs. <sub>Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; Identity ADR-1266</sub>
- **When code reinterprets a struct's fields as contiguous memory (for example with `Unsafe.As` or `MemoryMarshal.Cast`), declare the struct with an explicit `[StructLayout(LayoutKind.Sequential)]` or another explicit layout.** The reinterpreting code depends on the field layout, and the attribute records that layout as a contract. *Check:* Find `Unsafe.As<TStruct, T>`, `MemoryMarshal.Cast` or similar over a struct's fields and check that the struct has a `[StructLayout]` attribute. <sub>Identity ADR-1486</sub>
- **Back an optimization of a hot-path primitive (field, scalar or group arithmetic, encoders, constant-time helpers) with a benchmark in the benchmark projects. Quote before-and-after BenchmarkDotNet tables in the pull request, run in Release on one developer machine, and never run benchmarks in CI or gate merges on them.** Such optimizations need measured evidence, and shared CI runners give noisy numbers that prove nothing. *Check:* Look for diffs that micro-optimize such primitives without adding or updating a benchmark or quoting before-and-after tables, and for workflow steps that run benchmarks or gate on their results. <sub>Identity ADR-1266; Identity ADR-1386; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **In benchmark projects, make each benchmark class `public`, unsealed and marked `[MemoryDiagnoser]`, with inputs from a `Random` that has a fixed seed. Keep inputs that the measured method takes by `in` or fills by `out` in private fields, store results in a private auto-property instead of returning an `internal` type, and make `Main` return 1 when any benchmark fails so a `--job Dry` run works as a smoke check.** BenchmarkDotNet derives from the class, the memory diagnoser reports allocations, and a fixed seed gives the same inputs on every run. A ref target can't be a property, and a public method can't return an internal type. A run that ignores failures can't serve as a smoke check. *Check:* Look for sealed or non-public benchmark classes, a missing `[MemoryDiagnoser]`, unseeded randomness, benchmark methods that return internal types, `in`/`out` inputs held in properties, and a `Main` that doesn't check the summaries for failures. *Note:* Don't report private ref-target fields in a benchmark class as violations of the field-to-property analyzer rule. <sub>Identity ADR-1386</sub>
- **Load route-level containers in a frontend app shell through `React.lazy` inside a `Suspense` boundary, and make tests that assert on lazily loaded content wait for it with `findBy...` queries.** The shell paints before a surface loads, and a surface that is never visited is never downloaded. A synchronous `getBy` query runs before the lazy chunk resolves. *Check:* Look for static imports of route-level containers in app shells, and for tests that use `getBy` or `queryBy` on lazily loaded content. <sub>Identity ADR-1151</sub>
- **Make a client bundle that replaces a server-rendered page mount at once from data the server embedded in that page. Don't fetch data the host already knows before mounting, and don't re-theme the page when a later fetch returns.** While the bundle waits on the network, the user's typed or autofilled input, focus and choices are lost when the page is replaced, and a late reply themes the page a second time. *Check:* Look in mount or bootstrap code for a network request (a fetch or a query hook) that runs before `createRoot(...).render`, or that re-themes the page after the first render, for data the server could embed. <sub>Identity ADR-1253</sub>
- **Enable the ASP.NET Core Request Delegate Generator once in `Directory.Build.props`, and don't opt out per project except in a project that has a form-bound endpoint.** Generated delegates remove expression-tree compilation and JIT work for every endpoint at host start, which greatly shortens integration-test runs and production cold starts. *Check:* Flag a .csproj that sets `EnableRequestDelegateGenerator=false` without a form-bound endpoint, and flag a change that removes the shared setting. <sub>Identity ADR-1262</sub>
- **Only ask for a hand-written synchronous fast path on a `ValueTask`-returning method when the repository's design calls for it, when a benchmark shows the gain, or when the non-async form is just as simple. For example, a wait method can return `ValueTask.CompletedTask` when its task has already completed, and otherwise `new ValueTask(task.WaitAsync(cancellationToken))`. Otherwise don't report an `async ValueTask` method because its common path completes synchronously, and don't ask for it to be split into a wrapper and an async core.** An `async ValueTask` state machine is a struct that is boxed only when an await doesn't complete at once, so the synchronous path allocates nothing. Hot paths give up readability only for measured gains. *Check:* Before flagging the async overhead, check whether the method returns `ValueTask`, whether a design decision or benchmark asks for a fast path, and whether the non-async form is as simple as the async one. *Note:* Some sources ask for the fast path: one design decision returns a completed `ValueTask` for local-key signing, and one review asked for a non-async wait method. The reviews that declined the finding without a measurement are the default; those two cases are the exceptions listed in the statement. <sub>NCode.Disposables outcomes of #66; Randomness outcomes of #13; Identity ADR-1472; coordination outcomes of #20</sub>
- **Don't report a single small per-call allocation or parse (a `Uri` parse, an `AsyncLocal` restore scope, or the closure and delegate of a capturing lambda) on a path that already does much more work, such as an HTTP or provider round trip, unless a measurement shows it matters. Don't ask for capturing lambdas to be replaced with static lambdas and explicit state on such paths.** The cost can't be measured next to the surrounding work, while the fix adds state to transient types or threads a state parameter through every caller. *Check:* Before reporting, check the cost of the surrounding call, whether the work is needed on every call, and whether a benchmark or profile in the PR or issue shows allocation pressure. <sub>Identity outcomes of #600; coordination outcomes of #18</sub>
- **Don't report `string.Split` or substring allocations in code that runs once, such as startup parsing of a variable number of lines.** Allocation-free splitting is required only for strings with a fixed number of segments on per-call paths. *Check:* Before reporting allocating parsing, check whether the code runs on a per-call path and whether the string has a fixed number of segments. <sub>coordination outcomes of #31</sub>
- **Don't ask for per-call creation of an `HttpMessageInvoker` around `IHttpMessageHandlerFactory.CreateHandler` to be cached, or report it as a per-request handler allocation.** `CreateHandler` returns the cached handler of the name's active entry, so the only per-call cost is a small invoker that disposes nothing. Caching the invoker would break the handler rotation the factory manages. *Check:* Confirm that the handler comes from `IHttpMessageHandlerFactory` and that the invoker doesn't own it (`disposeHandler: false`). <sub>Identity outcomes of #722</sub>
- **Don't ask StackExchange.Redis code to switch from the text overload of `ScriptEvaluateAsync` to a prepared or loaded script for caching, unless the call passes `CommandFlags.NoScriptCache`.** The text overload already uses the client's script cache: it runs SCRIPT LOAD once, then EVALSHA, and resends the script after NOSCRIPT. *Check:* Before reporting that Lua source is resent on every call, check for `CommandFlags.NoScriptCache`. <sub>coordination outcomes of #31</sub>
- **Don't report a cache held by a singleton as unbounded, or as breaking a stateless-singleton rule, when its keys come only from configuration, correctness doesn't depend on it, and a recorded design decision accepts it.** It holds at most one entry per configured key, and a replica that misses or restarts just recomputes the value. *Check:* Trace where the keys come from, confirm that a miss only causes a recomputation, and look for the recorded exception. <sub>Identity outcomes of #520</sub>
- **Don't report an in-memory map or per-key history as a leak when its documentation accepts the bound and dropping entries would break a documented guarantee, such as a sequence that must never reuse a number or a replay window that resuming consumers rely on.** Capping or evicting entries would break the guarantee, and the memory is bounded or ends with the process. *Check:* Read the type's remarks, docs and changelog for the guarantee before asking for a cap or eviction. <sub>coordination outcomes of #19; coordination outcomes of #20</sub>
- **Don't report the allocation and O(n) copy of an enumerator that snapshots a collection under its lock, and don't suggest a version-counter snapshot cache, when the member's remarks document the cost and no measured hot enumeration path exists.** Snapshot enumeration is a deliberate thread-safety design, and a cache would add invalidation to every mutating member for a gain nobody has measured. *Check:* Read the `GetEnumerator` remarks and look for a benchmark or a caller that enumerates repeatedly on a hot path. <sub>NCode.Disposables outcomes of #66</sub>
- **Don't ask for collections to be frozen or copied on input parameter objects that are read once, or on result types built only internally from newly created collections.** No caller holds a mutable reference to them, so freezing would cost a copy per call and protect nothing. *Check:* Before reporting unowned collections, check whether the type is a one-shot input or is constructed only internally from new collections. <sub>Identity outcomes of #554</sub>
- **Don't ask for keyed single-row lookups to be replaced with loading a whole collection into memory when the operation is an infrequent operator action whose cost growth is documented as accepted. Don't report per-level store round trips in a cache-miss walk up a hierarchy that stops at the first cached ancestor, and don't propose reading the full lineage first instead.** Keyed single-row reads are cheap, while a bulk load reads far more than needed. A walk that stops at the first cached ancestor usually reads only the missing leaf. *Check:* Check whether each lookup is a keyed single-row read, how often the operation runs, whether the recursion returns at the first cache hit, and what the proposed bulk read would cost. <sub>Identity outcomes of #592; Identity outcomes of #599</sub>
- **Don't ask a read-only array parameter to become `IReadOnlyList<T>` when it is passed unchanged to a library API that requires an array. Don't ask a read-only text helper to take `ReadOnlySpan<char>` when every caller holds a string, the helper must handle null, or it is used as a method group.** The interface would force a copy on every call, and in those cases the span signature saves nothing or can't be used. *Check:* Look at the parameter's destination API and at the helper's callers and usages before reporting. <sub>coordination outcomes of #31; Randomness outcomes of #13</sub>
- **Don't ask for separate parameters to be combined into a composite value when they are computed once outside a loop and passing the composite would recompute them on every iteration.** The separate parameters exist to keep work, such as decoding, out of the loop. *Check:* Check whether the arguments are computed before the loop that calls the method and reused on each iteration. <sub>coordination outcomes of #21</sub>
- **Don't ask for a cheaper algorithm on a rarely run path when a design decision fixes the algorithm and no cost has been measured. Don't report a nested scan in test-only checking code when the test harness fixes small run sizes.** Changing the algorithm would break the decision it serves, such as every node computing the same result, and at fixed small sizes the cost can't be measured while an index would add a structure that has to stay in step with the scan. *Check:* Check for a design decision that fixes the algorithm, how often the path runs, and the harness's fixed run sizes. <sub>coordination outcomes of #22; coordination outcomes of #21</sub>
- **Don't ask for a background or concurrent call to be skipped up front because its result looks predictable when the called function makes its own early checks that the start condition would have to copy, and starting it costs little next to the work it runs alongside.** Skipping it up front copies the function's decision logic into a second place that has to stay in step, and saves only milliseconds. *Check:* Read the called function to confirm whether its answer really is known before it runs, and compare its start-up cost with the work it overlaps. <sub>project-template outcomes of #183</sub>
- **Don't report that per-key AWS KMS metadata calls (`ListResourceTags`, `DescribeKey`) made by an infrequent background sweep will throttle live cryptographic traffic.** AWS KMS counts those calls against quotas separate from the cryptographic-operation quota, so a sequential sweep can't throttle `Sign` or `Decrypt`. *Check:* Check which KMS quota the calls fall under and how often the sweep runs before reporting a throttling risk. <sub>Identity outcomes of #702</sub>
